subtopicTitle: Graphs — x-t, v-t, a-t; areas and slopes meaning

cards.front: On a position-time ($x-t$) graph, what physical quantity does the slope represent?
cards.back: The slope of an $x-t$ graph represents the **instantaneous velocity** ($v$). Mathematically, $v = \frac{dx}{dt}$.

cards.front: On a velocity-time ($v-t$) graph, what physical quantity does the slope represent?
cards.back: The slope of a $v-t$ graph represents the **instantaneous acceleration** ($a$). Mathematically, $a = \frac{dv}{dt}$.

cards.front: On a velocity-time ($v-t$) graph, what physical quantity does the area under the curve represent?
cards.back: The area under the curve of a $v-t$ graph represents the **displacement** ($\Delta x$) of the object. Mathematically, $\Delta x = \int v(t) dt$.

cards.front: On an acceleration-time ($a-t$) graph, what physical quantity does the area under the curve represent?
cards.back: The area under the curve of an $a-t$ graph represents the **change in velocity** ($\Delta v$) of the object. Mathematically, $\Delta v = \int a(t) dt$.

cards.front: Describe the motion of an object if its $x-t$ graph is a horizontal line.
cards.back: A horizontal line on an $x-t$ graph indicates that the object's position ($x$) is constant over time. This means the object is **at rest** (velocity $v=0$).

cards.front: Describe the motion of an object if its $v-t$ graph is a straight line with a positive, constant slope.
cards.back: A straight line with a positive, constant slope on a $v-t$ graph indicates that the object has a **constant positive acceleration**. Its velocity is increasing linearly with time.

cards.front: Mathematically, how do you derive a $v-t$ graph from an $x-t$ graph, and an $a-t$ graph from a $v-t$ graph?
cards.back:
To get $v(t)$ from $x(t)$: Differentiate $x(t)$ with respect to time: $v(t) = \frac{dx}{dt}$. This corresponds to finding the slope of the $x-t$ graph at each point.
To get $a(t)$ from $v(t)$: Differentiate $v(t)$ with respect to time: $a(t) = \frac{dv}{dt}$. This corresponds to finding the slope of the $v-t$ graph at each point.

cards.front: Mathematically, how do you derive a $v-t$ graph from an $a-t$ graph, and an $x-t$ graph from a $v-t$ graph?
cards.back:
To get $v(t)$ from $a(t)$: Integrate $a(t)$ with respect to time: $v(t) = \int a(t) dt + C_v$, where $C_v$ is the initial velocity $v_0$. This corresponds to finding the area under the $a-t$ graph.
To get $x(t)$ from $v(t)$: Integrate $v(t)$ with respect to time: $x(t) = \int v(t) dt + C_x$, where $C_x$ is the initial position $x_0$. This corresponds to finding the area under the $v-t$ graph.

cards.front: What would a vertical line segment on an $x-t$ graph imply physically?
cards.back: A vertical line segment on an $x-t$ graph implies an infinite velocity ($v = \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}$ where $\Delta t \to 0$). This means the object instantly changes its position without any passage of time, which is **physically impossible** for any real object with finite mass.
